:::{#def-relative-efficiency}
#### Relative efficiency

Let $\hparam_a$ and $\hparam_b$ be two estimators of the same estimand $\param$.
The **relative efficiency**
[@wikipedia_efficiency_statistics] of $\hparam_a$ with respect to $\hparam_b$
is the ratio of their [pMSEs](estimation.qmd#def-mse),
the reference estimator's, that of $\hparam_b$, in the numerator:

$$\frac{\pMSE{\hparam_b}}{\pMSE{\hparam_a}}$$

:::

:::{#rem-source-relative-efficiency}
#### Source: Relative efficiency

@CaseBerg01 define the asymptotic version, through variances, in Def. 10.1.16 (p. 476);
this finite-sample form uses the mean squared error of their Def. 7.3.1 (p. 330).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-relative-efficiency}
#### Reading the relative efficiency

A relative efficiency above 1 means $\hparam_a$ is more accurate than $\hparam_b$,
and below 1 means it is less accurate.
For two [unbiased](estimation.qmd#def-unbiased) estimators the pMSEs are the variances
([pMSE equals bias squared plus variance](estimation.qmd#thm-mse-bias-variance), with zero bias),
so the relative efficiency is the ratio of the variances.
:::
